Tab Sync Behavior

Tab Sync is a State behavior that extends Core State to broadcast finalized FeatureCell state snapshots to other browser tabs via the native browser BroadcastChannel API , and to apply incoming snapshots from remote tabs directly to the local state without re-entering the pipeline.

This behavior operates at the State stage of the pipeline. It extends the standard state commit path by adding a post-commit broadcast step. When a finalized snapshot is committed locally, it is serialized and posted to a feature-scoped BroadcastChannel. Other tabs listening on the same channel receive the snapshot and apply it directly, bypassing resolve, merge, operators, filters, and reducers.

Tab Sync does not transform values, influence merge semantics, or participate in pipeline control flow beyond its broadcast and receive responsibilities. The FeatureCell continues to operate on plain, in-memory state. Cross-tab coordination occurs only at the commit boundary.

Critical Behavior

Tab Sync is a critical behavior. If the behavior does not have a valid license, the behavior reports the failure immediately. However, if the BroadcastChannel API is unavailable in the runtime environment, the behavior degrades gracefully — it continues to operate as standard Core State without broadcasting or receiving cross-tab messages. This allows applications running in SSR, Node.js, or restricted environments to use the same FeatureCell configuration without errors.

Required Controller

The Tab Sync system requires both the Tab Sync Controller and the Tab Sync State Behavior to be registered on the same FeatureCell. The controller handles initial cross-tab state negotiation — determining whether the new tab should adopt established state from a peer or proceed with its bootstrap state. The behavior manages ongoing cross-tab state broadcasting and reception after negotiation completes. Without the controller, the behavior cannot safely determine when to begin broadcasting.

Synchronization Contract

Tab Sync synchronizes committed FeatureCell State values and shared reset operations across browser tabs that share the same origin. Loading status, Error, global Error, Controller outcomes, and destruction remain local to the tab where they occur. A successful Pipeline execution broadcasts its committed State value. A failed Pipeline execution leaves peer tabs unchanged.

During initial synchronization, a new tab receives the last committed State value from an established peer. The receiving State begins with its loading status set to false and its Error set to null. Transient metadata from the peer tab is not inherited.

Degraded Mode

If the BroadcastChannel API or localStorage is unavailable, the Tab Sync Controller degrades gracefully — it immediately clears the negotiation cache and abstains, allowing the pipeline to proceed with bootstrap state. The behavior continues to operate as standard Core State. No errors are thrown and no pipeline execution is blocked. The FeatureCell functions normally as a single-tab state container.

This makes Tab Sync safe to use in server-side rendering (SSR), Node.js services, Deno, web workers, and any other runtime where browser-specific APIs are not present. The same FeatureCell configuration works across all environments without conditional logic or feature detection.

Channel Lifecycle

The BroadcastChannel remains open for the lifetime of the FeatureCell and is closed automatically on destroy. Each tab generates a unique identifier at construction time to distinguish local broadcasts from remote ones.

Learn More →

Broadcast Filtering

Not all state emission types are broadcast. Destroy, incoming pipeline, error, abort, and deny emission types are filtered from cross-tab propagation. The State changes produced by these emissions remain local to the originating tab and are not carried into a later broadcastable emission.

License Requirement

Tab Sync requires a valid license . License validation is performed asynchronously at construction time using the license token provided in the behavior context. If validation fails, the behavior is marked as unlicensed and the pipeline rejects it.

Learn More →
Cross-Tab Message Flow

When a local commitState produces a broadcastable snapshot, Tab Sync posts a message containing the feature cell key, the originating tab identifier, the isolated snapshot, and the emission type. The message is delivered asynchronously via the native browser BroadcastChannel to all other tabs sharing the same origin and channel name.

On the receiving side, the behavior filters incoming messages by tab identifier and feature cell key. Messages originating from the same tab or targeting a different feature cell are discarded silently. Valid remote snapshots are applied directly to the local state and emitted as a TabSync emission type without re-entering the pipeline.

Re-Broadcast Prevention

Received cross-tab snapshots are committed through the parent super.commitState path, which bypasses the broadcast override entirely. Because the override is only invoked by the local pipeline commit path, incoming remote snapshots are never re-broadcast. This ensures that tab synchronization does not produce infinite broadcast loops between tabs.

The channel name is scoped per feature cell using a fixed prefix and the feature cell key. This ensures that different feature cells within the same origin maintain independent synchronization channels.

Diagrams
Configuration

Tab Sync is opt-in per and not a global feature. Cross-tab synchronization is not enabled at the application level — only FeatureCell instances that explicitly attach withTabSyncStateBehavior will participate in cross-tab broadcasting. All other feature cells continue to operate with standard, tab-local state management.

Tab Sync does not accept runtime configuration options. Its behavior is fully defined and deterministic, providing automatic cross-tab broadcasting, channel management, and lifecycle teardown by default.

Configuration consists solely of attaching the Tab Sync behavior to a FeatureCell in place of the default Core State behavior. When present, Tab Sync replaces Core State and automatically participates in the State stage with cross-tab synchronization capabilities.

Tab Sync inherits all state management semantics from Core State, including snapshot isolation, emission classification, and lifecycle management. The only addition is the post-commit broadcast step and the cross-tab receive listener.

Behavior Description

withTabSyncStateBehavior

Type: TabSyncState

Stage: State

Extends Core State to broadcast finalized state snapshots to other browser tabs via BroadcastChannel and applies incoming remote snapshots directly to the local state without re-entering the pipeline.

This behavior requires a valid Vault license. The channel is opened at construction time and closed automatically on destroy.

FeatureCell Initialization

The Tab Sync behavior is attached directly during FeatureCell definition and is not configured through a fluent API. This behavior is registered once, at construction time, as part of the FeatureCell's structural pipeline configuration.

Because this behavior replaces the default Core State behavior and manages a BroadcastChannel lifecycle, it must be present before any pipeline execution begins. Attaching it at definition time ensures that all committed state is consistently broadcast and that cross-tab messages are received from the moment the FeatureCell is initialized.

This design ensures deterministic synchronization behavior and prevents runtime mutation of cross-tab coordination rules. The behavior opens its channel on instantiation and closes it automatically on destroy.

Tab Identity and Broadcast Targeting

Each FeatureCell instance receives a unique tab identifier (called a conductor ID) generated automatically at construction time via crypto.randomUUID(). This identifier is ephemeral — it exists only for the lifetime of the page and is never persisted to storage. When a tab is closed or the page is reloaded, a new identifier is generated. When a tab is duplicated, the cloned tab receives its own fresh identifier because the ID is generated in-memory, not read from storage.

The tab identifier is included in every broadcast message. Receiving tabs use it to distinguish remote messages from their own and to identify which tab originated a given state change. This opens the door for application-level logic that targets or filters broadcasts based on the originating tab.

Filtering Broadcasts by Tab

By default, Tab Sync applies all valid remote snapshots to the local state. In some scenarios, applications may want to selectively process broadcasts based on which tab sent them. The tab identifier makes this possible by providing a consistent origin reference for the lifetime of the page.

Common scenarios where broadcast filtering by tab is useful:

  • Admin versus user tabs — an administrative tab broadcasts configuration changes, but other admin tabs should ignore those broadcasts to avoid overwriting in-progress edits.
  • Primary/secondary tab patterns — only one tab acts as the primary data source while secondary tabs consume its broadcasts, preventing conflicting writes from multiple tabs.
  • Selective feature sync — a dashboard tab broadcasts summary state, but a detail-view tab filters out those broadcasts because it manages its own granular state independently.
  • Debugging and diagnostics — during development, a developer can log or inspect broadcasts from a specific tab identifier to trace cross-tab state flow without noise from other open tabs.
  • Conflict resolution — when multiple tabs commit overlapping state changes, application logic can use tab identifiers to implement last-writer-wins, priority-based, or merge-based conflict strategies.
In-Memory Only

The tab identifier is generated in-memory and is never transmitted to a server or persisted to any storage mechanism. It exists solely for client-side coordination between browser tabs sharing the same origin.

Broadcast Payload and Platform Considerations

Full-State Broadcasts

Tab Sync broadcasts the entire synchronized state snapshot (StateSnapshotShape), not a delta or diff of what changed. Each broadcast message contains the complete committed State value at the time of the successful Pipeline execution. Receiving tabs replace their synchronized State value with the incoming value while retaining tab-local operational metadata.

This design eliminates the need for ordered message delivery, diff reconciliation, or sequence tracking between tabs. Every broadcast is self-contained and idempotent — a receiving tab can apply any single message and arrive at a consistent state regardless of how many prior messages it may have missed.

Tab-Local Operational State

Loading status and Error describe work performed by one tab. They are not synchronized, even when that work later produces a successful committed State value. Peer tabs receive the committed value without inheriting the originating tab's loading or Error lifecycle.

Data Size Considerations

Because the full state is serialized on every broadcast, large state trees produce proportionally larger messages on the BroadcastChannel. The browser's structured clone algorithm handles serialization, and there is no hard message size limit imposed by the specification. However, very large payloads can increase memory pressure and serialization time across all open tabs.

For feature cells managing large datasets, consider the following strategies to manage broadcast overhead:

  • Keep synchronized state focused and minimal — store only the data that other tabs need to reflect, not the entire application model.
  • Use separate feature cells for large, tab-local data that does not need cross-tab synchronization.
  • Profile broadcast frequency and payload size during development to identify potential bottlenecks before they reach production.

Platform Compatibility

Tab Sync relies on the native browser BroadcastChannel API. This API is supported in all modern browsers, including Chrome, Firefox, Edge, and Safari (from version 15.4). However, it is not available in all TypeScript runtime environments.

is a TypeScript library and can run in any environment that executes TypeScript — including Node.js, Deno, server-side rendering frameworks, and web workers. When the BroadcastChannel API is not available in the runtime, the behavior silently skips channel creation and operates as standard Core State. All state management continues to function normally — only cross-tab broadcasting and receiving are disabled.

This graceful degradation means applications can use the same FeatureCell configuration across browser, SSR, and server environments without conditional logic or runtime feature detection. When running in a browser, Tab Sync activates automatically. When running elsewhere, the behavior falls back to core state seamlessly.

Universal Configuration

There is no need to conditionally attach withTabSyncStateBehavior based on the runtime environment. The behavior detects the availability of BroadcastChannel at construction time and adapts accordingly. In non-browser environments, the behavior operates as standard Core State seamlessly.

DevTools Monitoring

Tab Sync operates entirely outside the pipeline. When a remote snapshot arrives via BroadcastChannel, it is applied directly to the local state and emitted as a TabSync emission — it does not pass through the pipeline stages. As a result, cross-tab state updates produce no additional pipeline messages in the DevTools.

This is by design. The DevTools trace pipeline execution to help engineers understand how state transitions flow through the behavioral pipeline. Because Tab Sync bypasses the pipeline entirely, there is no execution to trace. The received snapshot is treated as an authoritative external update — equivalent to a finalized state that has already completed its pipeline journey in the originating tab.

Engineers monitoring cross-tab behavior should be aware of the following:

  • Originating tab — the tab that commits state will show normal pipeline traces in DevTools (incoming, resolve, merge, filter, reduce, finalize). The broadcast occurs as a post-commit side effect and is not itself a traced operation.
  • Receiving tab — the tab that receives the remote snapshot will reflect the updated state in its observable stream, but no pipeline trace will appear in DevTools because no pipeline was executed.
  • State timeline — the DevTools state timeline will not show cross-tab snapshot arrivals. Because Tab Sync bypasses the pipeline, there is no traced emission to record. Engineers debugging cross-tab state flow should observe the receiving tab's state observable directly rather than relying on DevTools timeline entries.
Zero Noise Guarantee

Tab Sync adds no overhead to DevTools output. Whether an application synchronizes one feature cell or dozens across tabs, the DevTools pipeline view remains clean and focused exclusively on locally initiated state transitions. Cross-tab arrivals update the observable stream silently, keeping signal-to-noise ratio high during debugging.

Examples

Example 1: Use the Tab Sync Behavior in a FeatureCell

This example demonstrates a FeatureCell configured with the withTabSyncStateBehavior . When state updates are committed, the finalized snapshot is broadcast to all other browser tabs sharing the same origin.

Tab Sync extends Core State and broadcasts finalized snapshots as a post-commit side effect. It does not transform values, influence merge semantics, or participate in pipeline control flow. 

{{`// app.config.ts

import { ApplicationConfig } from '@angular/core';
import { provideVault, provideFeatureCell } from '@sdux-vault/angular';
import { withTabSyncStateBehavior, withTabSyncController } from '@sdux-vault/core';
import { EmployeeService } from './employee.service';

export const appConfig: ApplicationConfig = {
  providers: [
    provideVault({ logLevel: 'off' }),

    provideFeatureCell(
      EmployeeService,
      {
        key: 'employees',
        initialState: []
      },
      [
        // Enable cross-tab state synchronization
        withTabSyncStateBehavior
      ],
      [
        // Tab Sync Controller handles initial negotiation
        withTabSyncController
      ]
    )
  ]
};

// employee.service.ts

import { Injectable } from '@angular/core';
import { FeatureCell, injectVault } from '@sdux-vault/angular';
import { Employee } from './employee.shape';

@FeatureCell`}}<Employee[]>{{`('employees')
@Injectable({ providedIn: 'root' })
export class EmployeeService {
  readonly vault = injectVault`}}<Employee[]>{{`(EmployeeService);

  constructor() {
    this.vault.initialize();
  }

  addEmployee(): void {
    // State is committed locally and broadcast to other tabs
    this.vault.mergeState({
      value: [{ id: 1, name: 'Jane Doe' }]
    });
  }
}`}}
 
{{`import { FeatureCell } from '@sdux-vault/core';
import { withTabSyncStateBehavior, withTabSyncController } from '@sdux-vault/core';
import { Employee } from './employee.shape';

export const employeeCell = FeatureCell`}}<Employee[]>{{`(
  {
    key: 'employees',
    initialState: [],
  },
  [
    // Enable cross-tab state synchronization
    withTabSyncStateBehavior
  ],
  [
    // Tab Sync Controller handles initial negotiation
    withTabSyncController
  ]
);

// Initialize the FeatureCell
employeeCell.initialize();

// State is committed locally and broadcast to other tabs
employeeCell.mergeState({
  value: [{ id: 1, name: 'Jane Doe' }]
});`}}

Example 2: Receiving State from Another Tab

When another tab commits state to the same feature cell, the local tab automatically receives the updated snapshot and emits it as a TabSync emission. No additional configuration is required. Consumers observe the synchronized state through the standard state observable. 

{{`// Tab A commits state
this.vault.mergeState({
  value: [{ id: 1, name: 'Jane Doe' }]
});

// Tab B automatically receives the updated snapshot
// via the standard state signal
console.info(this.vault.state.value());
// → [{ id: 1, name: 'Jane Doe' }]`}}
 
{{`// Tab A commits state
employeeCell.mergeState({
  value: [{ id: 1, name: 'Jane Doe' }]
});

// Tab B automatically receives the updated snapshot
employeeCell.state$.subscribe(snapshot => {
  console.info(snapshot.value);
  // → [{ id: 1, name: 'Jane Doe' }]
});`}}
React Render Subscription

React components render Tab Sync State through useSyncExternalStore(). Initialize the FeatureCell in its owning module before the component renders. The method reads the current Snapshot during render, including State committed by the Tab Sync negotiation during initialization, and connects the component to subsequent State changes.

Do not create a separate state$ subscription or call initialize() from a React effect for this render path. The owning module controls initialization, while the component owns only its render subscription: 

{{`// employeeCell uses FeatureCell from '@sdux-vault/react'.
export function EmployeeView() {
  const snapshot = employeeCell.useSyncExternalStore();

  if (!snapshot.hasValue) {
    return <p>No synchronized State is available.</p>;
  }

  return <pre>{JSON.stringify(snapshot.value, null, 2)}</pre>;
}`}}

Example 3: Pairing Tab Sync with Persistence

Tab Sync can be combined with persist and encryption behaviors to achieve cross-tab synchronization, durable storage, and at-rest encryption. When all three behaviors are configured, state is encrypted, persisted locally, and broadcast to other tabs in a single commit cycle. It is never advised to persist state to local storage without encryption. 

{{`// app.config.ts

import { ApplicationConfig } from '@angular/core';
import { provideVault, provideFeatureCell } from '@sdux-vault/angular';
import { withTabSyncStateBehavior, withTabSyncController } from '@sdux-vault/core';
import { withAes256EncryptBehavior } from '@sdux-vault/addons';
import { withLocalStoragePersistBehavior } from '@sdux-vault/core';
import { EmployeeService } from './employee.service';

export const appConfig: ApplicationConfig = {
  providers: [
    provideVault({ logLevel: 'off' }),

    provideFeatureCell(
      EmployeeService,
      {
        key: 'employees',
        initialState: []
      },
      [
        // Cross-tab synchronization
        withTabSyncStateBehavior,
        // AES-256-GCM encryption for persisted state
        withAes256EncryptBehavior,
        // Durable local storage persistence
        withLocalStoragePersistBehavior
      ],
      [
        // Tab Sync Controller handles initial negotiation
        withTabSyncController
      ]
    )
  ]
};`}}
 
{{`import { FeatureCell } from '@sdux-vault/core';
import { withTabSyncStateBehavior, withTabSyncController } from '@sdux-vault/core';
import { withAes256EncryptBehavior } from '@sdux-vault/addons';
import { withLocalStoragePersistBehavior } from '@sdux-vault/core';
import { Employee } from './employee.shape';

export const employeeCell = FeatureCell`}}<Employee[]>{{`(
  {
    key: 'employees',
    initialState: [],
  },
  [
    // Cross-tab synchronization
    withTabSyncStateBehavior,
    // AES-256-GCM encryption for persisted state
    withAes256EncryptBehavior,
    // Durable local storage persistence
    withLocalStoragePersistBehavior
  ],
  [
    // Tab Sync Controller handles initial negotiation
    withTabSyncController
  ]
);`}}
